title: Altered Mental Status
hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is an elderly patient with a history of chronic alcoholism who presents to the emergency department with altered mental status following a recent fall. The patient has had episodic confusion and fluctuating consciousness since the fall. The subdural hematoma risk is elevated due to advanced age and chronic alcohol use, both of which contribute to brain atrophy and increased tension on bridging veins. Time is critical — expanding hematoma may cause mass effect and progressive neurological deterioration.

stacks.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
stacks.finding: The general examination is extremely useful to determine how sick the patient looks.

stacks.label: Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs
stacks.finding: It's important to look for lung pathology.

stacks.label: Physical Exam: Abdomen
stacks.finding: It's important to look for abdominal pathology.

stacks.label: Physical Exam: Neuro / Psych
stacks.finding: This is the patient's chief complaint — neurologic exam is essential.

stacks.label: CBC with differential
stacks.finding: CBC is always a good screening tool in nearly every patient.

stacks.label: TSH, serum
stacks.finding: TSH screens for abnormal thyroid levels which could contribute to altered mental status.

stacks.label: CT of head without contrast
stacks.finding: CT without contrast is the order of choice. With possible head trauma, rule out intracranial bleed. CT with contrast makes it difficult to distinguish contrast from hemorrhage. CT preferred for speed; MRI more sensitive but slower.

stacks.label: Basic metabolic profile / Comprehensive metabolic profile / Liver function panel
stacks.finding: Chemistries are an important screening tool to reach a diagnosis.

stacks.label: CT, head, with contrast
stacks.finding: CT with contrast makes it difficult to distinguish between contrast enhancement and intracranial hemorrhage. Non-contrast CT is the correct choice for suspected bleed.

stacks.label: Consult, surgery, neurologic / Craniotomy
stacks.finding: Neurosurgery should be consulted to evacuate the subdural hematoma. Craniotomy for evacuation.

physical_exam.neurological: Fluctuating level of consciousness. Assess for lateralizing signs, pupil asymmetry, and GCS. Focal deficits may indicate mass effect from expanding hematoma.
physical_exam.heent: Assess for signs of head trauma or skull fracture.
physical_exam.psychiatric: Altered mental status — differentiate from psychiatric etiology.

decoys.label: CT head with contrast
decoys.reason_wrong: Contrast makes it difficult to distinguish blood from enhancement. Non-contrast CT is required for suspected intracranial hemorrhage.

decoys.label: Lumbar puncture
decoys.reason_wrong: LP is contraindicated with suspected mass effect from intracranial hemorrhage — risk of herniation.

decoys.label: EEG
decoys.reason_wrong: While seizure is on the differential, CT head takes priority given history of fall and AMS.

teach_me_steps.reasoning: First-line imaging for suspected intracranial hemorrhage. Non-contrast is essential — contrast obscures blood. CT faster than MRI.
Subdural hematoma with mass effect requires surgical evacuation. Time is brain.
Elderly patient with AMS and surgical pathology requires admission, not ER discharge.

case_summary: Elderly alcoholic patient with fall → subdural hematoma. Subdurals result from venous bleeding after blunt head trauma — bridging veins rupture. Risks: advanced age, alcoholism, anticoagulation. CT without contrast → neurosurgery for evacuation.
